title: Stock Indices
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/0/body: A **stock index** shows how a basket of stocks is doing with a single number. The **S&P 500** covers 500 large US companies, the **Nasdaq 100** covers 100 large non-financial companies on the Nasdaq exchange with a heavy tech weighting, and the **DAX** covers 40 large German companies.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/0/tip: Index symbol names differ between brokers (like US500, SPX500, NAS100, US100, GER40 or DE40).
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/2/body: Indices move in **points**, but to compare two indices, **percent** matters more. The same 100 points on an index at 5,000 is **2%**, but on an index at 20,000 it's only **0.5%**.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/2/tip: The value of each point in index CFDs depends on your broker and size. Check it before you trade.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/3/prompt: The Nasdaq 100 went from 18,000 to 18,360. By what percent did it rise?
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/4/prompt: You have a long position on the S&P 500 where each point is worth $5. The index rose 40 points. How much did you make?
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/4/explanation: 40 points × $5 = $200. If the index had dropped 40 points, you'd have lost the same amount.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/5/statement: The DAX is an index of 500 large European companies.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/5/explanation: The DAX is an index of 40 large German companies traded on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange. The famous 500-company index is the US S&P 500.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/6/body: Indices are the market's **risk-mood thermometer**. In **risk-on**, stocks usually rise. In **risk-off**, stocks usually fall, money flows to safe-haven assets, and the **VIX** (the fear index) goes up.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/6/example/rows/: Stocks ↑ · AUD ↑ · yen and franc weaker
Stocks ↓ · yen, franc and gold stronger
From S&P 500 options; rises with fear
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/6/tip: These are common tendencies, not fixed rules.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/7/prompt: This S&P 500 chart is from a day the VIX spiked. Which read fits the chart?
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/7/explanation: Highs and lows keep getting lower and the bearish candles are big. Together with a VIX spike, this is the picture of a risk-off day.
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/8/prompt: On a day of heavy risk-off, which combination is more likely?
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/8/options/0: Stocks fall and the Japanese yen strengthens
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/8/options/1: Stocks rise and the Japanese yen weakens
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/8/options/2: The Australian dollar rises and gold falls
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/8/options/3: The Nasdaq rises and the VIX falls
lessons/gold-u3-l1/steps/8/explanation: In risk-off, stocks get sold and money flows to safe havens like the yen. The other options describe a risk-on day.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/0/body: Since about 2020, Bitcoin has often shown a **positive correlation** with stock indices, especially the **Nasdaq**, meaning they often moved in the same direction. But this correlation **isn't fixed**, and sometimes it weakens or disappears.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/0/tip: Correlation means moving together statistically, not that one causes the other to move.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/1/statement: Bitcoin's correlation with the Nasdaq is a fixed rule that always holds.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/1/explanation: Correlation between assets changes over time. There have been periods when Bitcoin and the Nasdaq moved independently or even in opposite directions.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/2/body: In several **heavy risk-off** episodes, like the March 2020 crash and the 2022 sell-offs, crypto behaved like a **risky asset** and fell along with stocks, not like gold. That's why many traders also check the **Nasdaq and the VIX** before trading crypto.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/2/tip: Bitcoin is called "digital gold", but in several major crises it behaved more like a tech stock.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/3/prompt: The Nasdaq dropped 3% on recession fears, and the highlighted candle formed on Bitcoin at the same time. Which read fits this behavior?
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/3/options/0/lab: Crypto fell with stocks as a risky asset
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/3/options/1/lab: Crypto rose as a safe haven
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/3/explanation: A big bearish candle at the same time as the Nasdaq drop means Bitcoin was sold as a risky asset in this risk-off move.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/4/prompt: In heavy risk-off, which two assets usually fall together?
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/4/options/2: The Japanese yen and the Swiss franc
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/4/explanation: The Nasdaq and Bitcoin are both risky assets and usually get sold when fear hits. Gold, the yen and the franc usually attract buyers, and the VIX goes up.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/5/body: The stock market is closed on weekends, but crypto trades **24 hours a day, 7 days a week**. That's why crypto is sometimes the **first market** to react to weekend news. US index futures also reopen on **Sunday evening, New York time**.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/6/prompt: The Nasdaq is in a strong downtrend, the VIX is high, and after defending 60,000 twice, Bitcoin has now closed below it. What do you do?
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/6/explanation: The risk-off mood lines up with a lower high and a support break, so a continued drop is more likely. But breakouts are sometimes fake, so you need a stop loss above the broken level.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/7/sentence: Crypto trades ___ days a week, but the US stock market is ___ on weekends.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/7/explanation: Crypto never closes, but stock exchanges are shut on weekends. That's why crypto sometimes reacts to news first.
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/8/prompt: Big geopolitical news breaks on Saturday and Bitcoin drops 5%. Where will you most likely see US indices react first?
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/8/options/0: Index futures, from Sunday evening New York time
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/8/options/1: The stock market, Saturday at 9:30 New York time
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/8/options/2: Only on Tuesday, after the stock market closes
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/8/options/3: Nowhere; weekend news doesn't affect stocks
lessons/gold-u3-l2/steps/8/explanation: The stock market is closed until Monday at 9:30, but index futures open on Sunday evening, and that's where you'll see stocks react first. Of course, a Bitcoin drop doesn't necessarily mean indices will drop.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/0/body: The US stock market (NYSE and Nasdaq) is open from **9:30 to 16:00 New York time**. Depending on US daylight saving time, it opens at around **13:30 or 14:30 UTC**. The **DAX** trades on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange's Xetra system from **9:00 to 17:30 German time**.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/0/tip: At many brokers, index CFDs are priced almost around the clock, but volume is usually highest during regular market hours.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/1/body: A **gap** means the opening price is away from the previous close. In indices, gaps usually show up after **overnight news**, **big companies' earnings reports** or the **weekend**.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/2/prompt: Tap the candle where the market opened with a gap down.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/2/explanation: This candle opened far below the previous candle's close, with no prices traded in between: a gap down. The other candles opened right where the previous one closed.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/3/prompt: The S&P 500 closed at 5,000 yesterday and opened at 4,940 today. How big is the gap?
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/4/prompt: Put the parts of a US trading day in time order.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/4/explanation: Pre-market runs before 9:30 with low volume, then the market opens and closes at 16:00. Many earnings reports come out after hours and can create the next day's gap.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/5/body: If price gaps past your stop loss, your order usually fills at the **first available price**, and your loss can be **bigger than planned**. Holding an index position over the **weekend** or before big companies' **earnings reports** carries gap risk.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/5/tip: Many traders wait for a "gap fill", but there's no guarantee that every gap gets filled.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/6/statement: Every gap in the indices is sure to fill the same day.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/6/explanation: Some gaps fill quickly, but gaps driven by big news can take days or never fill at all. Trading only on the hope of a gap fill, without a stop loss, is dangerous.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/7/prompt: You bought the Nasdaq 100 at $2 per point: entry 18,000, stop loss 17,900. After overnight news, the market opens at 17,800 and your stop loss fills right there. How much did you lose?
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/7/explanation: From entry to the fill price is 200 points: 200 × 2 = $400, while the plan was 100 points × 2 = $200. That's gap risk.
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/8/prompt: It's Friday afternoon and you have a long position open on the DAX. A major election with an uncertain outcome is happening over the weekend. What's the most sensible move?
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/8/options/0: Cut your size or close part of the position before the close
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/8/options/1: Double your size, since gaps always favor buyers
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/8/options/2: Remove your stop loss so the gap can't trigger it
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/8/options/3: Nothing; prices don't change over the weekend
lessons/gold-u3-l3/steps/8/explanation: The election result could open the market with a big gap, and your stop loss might fill at a worse price. Cutting your size keeps your gap risk in line with the risk you're willing to take.
